text: Carl Wilhelmson's father, a naval master, died in a shipwreck in 1875. His mother opened a small shop to support the family. In 1881 Carl was apprenticed to the lithographers Meyer and Köster in Gothenburg, and he took evening classes at the School of Design and Crafts. Later he became a full-time student of Carl Larsson at the Valand Academy. Larsson and his former employers recommended him for a scholarship in 1888. He took photographs as an amateur.

François Forster won the Grand Prix de Rome in 1814. The king of Prussia, who was in Paris with the allies, gave him a gold medal and a pension of 1500 francs for two years. With that money he studied in Rome, mostly the works of Raphael. He was born in Le Locle in Switzerland and first studied under the engraver Pierre-Gabriel Langlois. In 1844 he succeeded Tardieu in the Académie des Beaux-Arts. He engraved historical subjects and portraits.

Gottlieb Welté came from Mainz and worked as an etcher and landscape painter. In Estonia, then part of the Russian Empire, he worked at Põltsamaa Castle and its porcelain manufacture from 1781 to 1784. He painted figures into large Põltsamaa landscapes and drew Estonian peasants. Then he worked as a home teacher at Võisiku manor. Most of his works are small. In Mainz and Frankfurt he was known mostly as an etcher and landscape painter.

Johann Friedrich Morgenstern came from a family of painters in Frankfurt. His father taught him, and he later went to Dresden to study. There he copied works by Johann Heinrich Roos and etched several sheets after his drawings. His own etchings show landscapes with figures and animals, as well as busts of old men and women. The Städel Collection and the Frankfurt Historical Museum hold his views of Old Frankfurt. He also restored damaged paintings.

Johann Gottfried Haid made mezzotint copies of old masters. His nephew Johann Elias Haid also became an engraver and took over the family publishing house of Haid and Son. One of the mezzotints credited to him shows Joseph II, Holy Roman Emperor, after a painting by Martin van Meytens. Another version of the same portrait comes from the circle of Meytens. Haid came from Augsburg. He lived from 1710 to 1776.

José Malhoa, with Columbano Bordalo Pinheiro, was the leading name in Portuguese naturalist painting in the second half of the 19th century. Both belonged to the Grupo do Leão in the 1880s. Malhoa often painted popular scenes, and his two most famous paintings are The Drunks and Fado. He stayed faithful to naturalism. A few works, such as Autumn, show impressionist influences. He was born in Caldas da Rainha.

Thomas Hicks painted a portrait of Abraham Lincoln that was engraved by Leopold Grozelier. He came from Newtown, Bucks County, Pennsylvania, and became a portrait painter, though he is also known for genre works. In the late 1840s he studied with the French painter Thomas Couture. Among his pupils were George Bernard Butler and Charles Henry Yewell, and he painted genre scenes as well as portraits. He died in 1890.

Vincent Jansz van der Vinne was the great-grandson of the painter Vincent van der Vinne. He learned from his father, Jan Laurentsz van der Vinne, who painted flowers for bulb growers in Haarlem. In 1754 he joined the Haarlem Guild of St. Luke. He painted Italianate landscapes and flower still lifes, and he also made tapestries. From 1778 to 1785 he was the first curator of art at the new Teyler's Museum. Pieter Teyler's will had said that an artistic painter or other lover of the arts and sciences should live in his house.

Nevinson became one of the most famous war artists of the First World War. He studied at the Slade School of Art under Henry Tonks, alongside Stanley Spencer and Mark Gertler. After leaving he befriended Marinetti, the founder of Italian Futurism, and the radical writer and artist Wyndham Lewis. Lewis founded the short-lived Rebel Art Centre. Nevinson fell out with him and the other rebels when he attached their names to the Futurist movement. Friends called him Richard.

Charles Herbert Woodbury began teaching regularly while still a freshman at MIT, where he studied mechanical engineering. At nineteen he was the youngest member of the Boston Art Club. He had little formal art training, only a few months at the Académie Julian in Paris in 1891, and then he went to Holland to study the modern Dutch painters. He kept a winter studio in Boston and spent summers in Perkins Cove, Maine, where he founded a successful summer art colony school. In 1928 he helped found the Ogunquit Art Association.

Guillaume Vogels was the son of a laborer and worked as a house painter before he owned his own decorating company in Brussels. One of his employees, the Greek painter Périclès Pantazis, became his lifelong friend and showed him the palette knife. His first exhibition, in Ghent, was not well received by critics. His career turned only in 1880, when he took part in the Paris Salon. In 1884 he joined Les XX, which led to a meeting with James Ensor. He left his works undated.

Jan van Os started out painting seascapes and became known for fruit and flower still lifes. He painted his flowers in the style of Jan van Huysum, usually on a marble ledge against a green background. He came from Middelharnis, studied with Aert Schouman in The Hague, and spent the rest of his life there. In 1775 he married Susanna de La Croix, a pastellist. Their children Pieter, Maria Margaretha and Georgius became artists too. He taught them himself.

Johann Rombauer came from a German family of nine children in Lőcse, now Levoča, and his father was a woodcarver. At nineteen he began working as a portraitist in Pest. A Polish aristocrat who met him in Bártfa was impressed by his talent and invited him to his estate near Romaniv. By 1806 he was teaching and painting in Saint Petersburg, where he became a member of the Imperial Academy of Arts. Vladimir Borovikovsky and Orest Kiprensky influenced his style. He returned to Hungary in 1824.

Janus la Cour was introduced to painting at the Aarhus Latin School by Emmerik Høegh-Guldberg and his apprentice Christen Købke. In Copenhagen he studied privately with Wilhelm Marstrand and then with Skovgaard, who became a personal friend. From 1861 to 1884 he lived with the Skovgaard family. On trips to Italy he painted Lake Nemi and Tivoli, and in Denmark he painted eastern Jutland, often in rainy or stormy weather. He kept away from the Copenhagen scene. Statens Museum for Kunst holds several of his paintings.

Joseph Badger began as a house painter and glazier and kept at that work all his life, along with painting signs and heraldic devices, to earn a living when orders for portraits slackened. He was born in Charlestown, Massachusetts, the son of a tailor. In 1731 he married Katharine Felch, and they moved to Boston around 1733. He belonged to the Brattle Street Church. He died in Boston in 1765.

Martín Rico stayed true to painting out of doors throughout his life, even as his style changed. He trained at the Real Academia de San Fernando under Jenaro Pérez Villaamil, the academy's first professor of landscape painting. In 1860 a government scholarship took him to Paris. There he looked to the Barbizon painters, Charles-François Daubigny above all. The Franco-Prussian War sent him back to Spain at the end of 1870. He died in Venice.

Nikolay Mosolov was the son of an etcher and print collector, and he became known for his etchings after the Old Masters. He studied under Fyodor Iordan at the Imperial Academy of Arts in St. Petersburg. He finished his education in Dresden and Paris, where he worked in the studio of Léopold Flameng and won his first gold medal for etchings. In 1872 he published in French a set of etchings after paintings in the Hermitage. He signed them with the French form of his name, Massaloff. He worked in Moscow.

Wolfgang Heimbach was deaf and mute, but he could read and write several languages. In Italy he worked for the noble houses of Doria Pamphilj and Medici. He later served as court painter to King Frederick III of Denmark-Norway and, from 1670, to the Prince Bishop of Münster. His most important work is the homage to Frederik III, which shows the event in an almost photographic way. Heimbach painted himself in the foreground next to the inscription, waving his hat triumphantly.

August Querfurt painted soldiers and battle scenes. His father Tobias Querfurt, who painted landscapes and animals, gave him his first lessons. He then studied under Rugendas at Augsburg. He painted encampments and battles, as well as hunting subjects. He sometimes imitated Bourguignon, Parrocel and Van der Meulen, but he tried above all to form his style on Wouwerman. The Belvedere Museum has two hunting pieces by him, and he died in Vienna in 1761.

Bartolomeo Vivarini sometimes drew a goldfinch as his signature, since vivarino means goldfinch in Italian. His brother Antonio and his nephew Alvise were painters too. He learned oil painting from Antonello da Messina, and he is said to have made the first oil picture done in Venice in 1473, a large altarpiece in nine parts for San Zanipolo. Most of his other works are in tempera. The Getty, the Louvre, the National Gallery in London and the Uffizi are among the collections that hold his work.

Francesco di Giorgio Martini built almost seventy fortifications for Federico da Montefeltro of Urbino, including city walls and early star-shaped forts. He was born in Siena and trained as a painter under Vecchietta. His cassone panels show wedding processions in vast, almost empty cities drawn in perspective. He also wrote a treatise on architecture, engineering and military art, which he worked on for decades and finished after 1482. Leonardo da Vinci owned a copy and filled it with notes and sketches.

Franciszek Smuglewicz spent 21 years in Rome, where he studied under Anton von Maron and embraced the Neo-Classical style. A royal scholarship from King Stanisław August Poniatowski helped him, and he took part in cataloging artifacts from Nero's Domus Aurea. In 1784 he returned to Warsaw and founded a school of fine arts. He is considered a founder of the Vilnius school of art. His students included Jan Rustem and Józef Oleszkiewicz. His father Łukasz and his brother Antoni were painters too.

John Ottis Adams grew up in central Indiana but trained in London at the South Kensington School of Art, then spent seven years in Germany at the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich. He is best known as a member of the Hoosier Group of Indiana landscape painters. With William Forsyth he formed the Muncie Art School, which closed after two years. He taught at the John Herron Art Institute in Indianapolis and gave informal lessons at the Hermitage, his home and studio near Brookville. In 1896 he was among those who formed the Society of Western Artists.

Jacob van Hulsdonck moved from Antwerp to Middelburg at a young age and probably got part of his training there. The leading still life studio in Middelburg belonged to Ambrosius Bosschaert. Hulsdonck probably did not train with him, but he may have influenced Bosschaert's early work. By 1608 he was back in Antwerp and a master in the Guild of Saint Luke. He had seven children. Roughly 100 paintings are attributed to him, and his careful handling of detail likely explains why there are so few.

John Russell trained under Francis Cotes, one of the pioneers of English pastel painting. At 19 he converted to Methodism and made no secret of it, trying to preach and convert at every opportunity. That caused tension with his family and his teacher. He set up his own studio in London in 1767. Selina, Countess of Huntingdon, tried to persuade him to give up painting and attend her Methodist ministers' training college in Wales, but she did not succeed. In 1772 he wrote Elements of Painting with Crayons.

Paul Berthon made colored lithograph posters in the Art Nouveau style, much like his contemporary Alphonse Mucha. Most of them contained no advertising and were meant to stand on their own. He studied painting with Luc-Olivier Merson, but his lessons in decorative arts with Eugène Grasset influenced him far more. Strong lines mark his prints. His posters appear in the series Les Maîtres de l'Affiche, and he also designed its cover.

Richard Brakenburgh painted merry-makings and drunken assemblies, the same subjects as Bernard Schendel. Houbraken called him a light-hearted poet. He was a pupil of Hendrik Mommers, who painted clever genre scenes in the manner of Adriaen van Ostade. Some said he was a pupil of Schendel, but the two were the same age and painted in similar styles. The RKD registers him in Leeuwarden from 1670 to 1687. He did well enough that his Frisian widow could buy an annuity.

William Woollett came from a family that had emigrated from the Dutch Republic to England. He was born in Maidstone. He was apprenticed to the Fleet Street engraver John Tinney and studied at the St Martin's Lane academy. His first important plate, from Richard Wilson's Destruction of the Children of Niobe, was published by Boydell in 1761. A companion engraving after Wilson's Phaethon followed in 1763. He later engraved several of Benjamin West's pictures.

Alfred Stevens is best known for the monument to the Duke of Wellington in St Paul's Cathedral. He was the son of a decorator and joiner in Blandford Forum, and at ten he went into his father's workshop as an assistant. He never attended an English school. In 1833 the rector of his parish enabled him to go to Italy, where he spent nine years studying at Naples, Bologna, Siena, Pompeii and other places, among them Florence, where he studied for a time at the Accademia di Belle Arti.

Dufau began drawing in bed. Her father, of Basque ancestry, had made a fortune on a trip to Cuba. After her sisters married she wanted to study art, and the family moved to Paris in 1888. She enrolled at the Académie Julian and studied with William Bouguereau and Tony Robert-Fleury. In 1895 she won the Marie Bashkirtseff prize at the Salon des Artistes Français for L'Amour de l'Art. Poster commissions followed, among them one for La Fronde.

George Loring Brown first studied wood engraving under Alonzo Hartwell and worked as an illustrator. He was born in Boston. He studied painting with Washington Allston, but he soon went to Europe and lived mostly in Italy for years. Most of his pictures have Italian subjects, and there is nothing specifically American about them in treatment or sentiment. Among the best are Sunset in Genoa and Bay of Naples.

Giovanni Antonio Boltraffio worked in the studio of Leonardo da Vinci. He and Bernardino Luini were the strongest artistic personalities to come out of it. According to Vasari he came from an aristocratic family and was born in Milan. His major painting of the 1490s is a Resurrection that he made with another Leonardo pupil, Marco d'Oggiono, now in the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin. A Madonna and Child in the Museo Poldi Pezzoli in Milan is one of the high points of his career.

Giovanni Baglione is best remembered for his collection of biographies of the artists who worked in Rome during his lifetime. He also painted a great deal. His relationship with the younger Caravaggio was acrimonious, and it showed in both his art and his writings. He was born and died in Rome, but by his own account he came from a noble family of Perugia. He was a pupil of Francesco Morelli.

Jacques d'Arthois specialised in wooded landscapes with figures and often depicted the woods around his native Brussels. He also designed tapestries. He was one of the few 17th-century landscape painters from Brussels whose fame lasted, and many other landscape artists imitated his style. He was baptized in 1613 as the son of Henri Artois. In 1625 he became an apprentice to Jan Mertens, an artist whose work is not known.

James Craig Annan was the second son of the photographer Thomas Annan and joined the family firm in Glasgow. In 1883 he went to Vienna to learn photogravure from its inventor, Karel Klíč. He brought the process to Britain. The family firm became the leading gravure printer there. In 1894 he was elected to the Linked Ring, a select international group of art photographers. He was also made an Honorary Fellow of the Royal Photographic Society.

Katsukawa Shunsen began as a student of the Rimpa school artist Tsutsumi Tōrin III, under the name Shunrin. Around 1806 he became a student of Katsukawa Shun'ei and changed his name to Katsukawa Shunsen. In 1820 he succeeded Katsukawa Shunkō I and became Shunkō II. He is best known for genre scenes, landscapes and prints of beautiful women, made with Western-style perspective. In the late 1820s he stopped making woodblock prints and painted ceramics instead. He died about 1830.

Kazimierz Alchimowicz worked as an estate manager near Kyiv until he was banished to Siberia for six years of hard labor for taking part in the January Uprising. At Verkhoturye, beyond the Urals, he began drawing to relieve the monotony and sold drawings with nature motifs and religious themes. After he came back he studied in Warsaw under Wojciech Gerson and then at the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich. From 1876 to 1878 he lived in Paris and exhibited at the Salon. In 1880 he set up his own studio in Warsaw.

Lan Ying came from Hangzhou in Zhejiang province and painted landscapes, human figures, flowers and birds during the Ming dynasty. His style name was Tianshu, and he also used the pseudonyms Diesou and Shi Toutuo. His painting followed the style of Huang Gongwang and Wu Zhen. His son Lan Yu and his grandson Lan Shen became painters too. He lived from about 1585 to 1664.

Little is known about the life of Lucas Gassel. He probably moved from Deurne to Antwerp before 1520 and trained there, though his frequent court scenes suggest a stay in Brussels. He helped modernize the landscape tradition in Flanders. He also designed prints for the Antwerp publisher Hieronymus Cock. He was a humanist and a friend of Dominicus Lampsonius, who put him in his 1572 book of 23 engraved portraits of leading artists from the Low Countries. His earliest work dates from 1538.

Marie-Victoire Lemoine was the eldest of four sisters, and her sisters Marie-Denise Villers and Marie-Élisabeth Gabiou became painters too. Unlike them she never married, and she was one of the few women of her time who made a living through painting. In the early 1770s she studied with François-Guillaume Ménageot, and they lived and worked in a house next to the studio of Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun. She mainly painted portraits, miniatures and genre scenes. When she died at sixty-six she left only 10 francs in cash.

Martin Ferdinand Quadal worked all across Europe, in England, Italy, Austria, Holland, Germany, France and Russia. He came from Měrovice nad Hanou in Moravia and went to London at an early age. He studied in Vienna and Paris and became a student of François Boucher. The Prince de Condé employed him, and he was particularly successful in France for his paintings of horses. In 1779 he moved to Dublin and painted animal subjects, and the Dublin Society bought several of them for its students. In 1797 Emperor Paul I invited him to Saint Petersburg, where he died in 1811.

William Home Lizars first learned engraving as an apprentice to his father, a publisher and engraver, and then studied under John Graham at the Trustees' Academy in Edinburgh alongside David Wilkie. When his father died in 1812, he had to carry on the business to support his mother and family. Horatio McCulloch and Daniel Macnee worked for him. From 1819 his studio produced plates for natural history works, among them Prideaux John Selby's Illustrations of British Ornithology. In October 1826 he met John James Audubon in Edinburgh.

Carlo Labruzzi painted mainly landscapes and was born in Rome. In 1798 he was named a professor at the Academy of Fine Arts of Perugia, and he later became its director. He died in Perugia in December 1817, and Tommaso Minardi replaced him. His pupils there included Silvestro Massari, Margherita Lazi and Marianna Candidi Dionigi. He lived from 1748 to 1817.

Charles de Steuben moved with his father, an officer who entered Russian service, to Saint Petersburg at twelve, and studied drawing there at the Imperial Academy of Arts as a guest student. In 1802 he went with the young Grand Duchess Maria Pavlovna to Weimar and served as a page at the ducal court. The poet Friedrich Schiller, a family friend, saw his talent at once. In 1803 he traveled to Paris with a letter to the painter François Gérard, who took in many penniless students. He later painted scenes from the Napoleonic era, among them The Death of Napoleon.

Charles Théodore Bernier sometimes worked under the pseudonym Charles Dubailly. He was first known for engraved reproductions of Old Masters and later for portraits. He won the Prix de Rome in 1891, and a grant took him to Paris in 1892, where Léon Bonnat mentored him. After his father died in 1893 he came home to Angre and stayed there as a painter and engraver. He also promoted the local drama society. Émile Verhaeren became a firm friend after visiting the archaeological museum that Bernier's father had set up.

Évariste Vital Luminais is sometimes called the painter of the Gauls, because he is best known for works on early French history. He came from a family of lawyers and legislators in Nantes. His family sent him to Paris at 18, where he studied with Auguste Debay and later with Léon Cogniet. He made his official début at the Paris Salon of 1843 with two paintings. In 1869 he was awarded the Légion d'honneur. He was a founder member of the Société des Artistes Français.

Guillam Dubois joined the Haarlem Guild of St. Luke in 1646. In 1652 he went on a trip through Germany with fellow guild members Vincent van der Vinne, Dirck Helmbreeker, Joost Boelen and Cornelis Bega. They stayed a month with Abraham Cuyper in Cologne, and after Helmbreeker returned to Haarlem the rest went on to Frankfurt and Heidelberg. Van der Vinne recorded the months in his diary. The trip influenced Dubois's later landscapes, though he was also a follower of Cornelis Vroom. He died in Haarlem in 1661.

Henry Mosler moved to New York with his family at eight, and then to Cincinnati. His father had been a lithographer in Europe but worked as a cigar maker in America. In his early teens Henry was apprenticed to a wood engraver. During the Civil War he served as an art correspondent for Harper's Weekly and published 34 drawings in it, 18 of them about the Kentucky and Ohio Campaign. He also drew portraits of several generals. In 1863 he went to Düsseldorf, where he studied at the Royal Academy for almost three years.

John Inigo Richards was one of the founding members of the Royal Academy and served as its secretary from 1788 until his death. He studied at the St Martin's Lane Academy under George Lambert. Like Francis Hayman, he worked as a scene painter in London theatres, and he kept a lifelong interest in theatre design. He is credited with designing the Chestnut Street Theatre in Philadelphia for his brother-in-law Thomas Wignell. When he died he acknowledged a daughter born to the actress Ann Pitt, and left her a snuff box decorated with a picture of her mother.

Richard Ansdell lost his father young and was educated at the Liverpool Blue Coat school for orphans. After school he worked for a portrait painter in Liverpool and spent time as a sign painter in the Netherlands. His animal and rural subjects proved popular and soon brought wealthy patrons. He first showed at the Royal Academy in 1840, with Grouse Shooting and A Galloway Farm, and then exhibited there every year until 1885, 149 canvases in all. In 1841 he married Maria Romer. They had 11 children.

Tyko Sallinen grew up in Haparanda in a family strictly committed to Laestadianism. He ran away from home at 14 and supported himself as a tailor journeyman. His first wife, Helmi Vartiainen, called Mirri, was the model for many of his early fauvist paintings. They were married from 1909 to 1916. In late 1916 he became a founder member of the November Group, which brought together Finnish expressionists and cubists. He was one of the first Finnish modernists to stress emotion and individuality.

George Chambers was eight years old when he started working on the coal sloops in Whitby harbour. Local captains and crews were so impressed by his decorations on their ships that a ship-owner released him from his apprenticeship so he could paint full-time. In 1825 he worked his way to London on a trading vessel. His pictures hung in the parlour of the Waterman's Arms in Wapping, and the sailors liked them. King William IV and Queen Adelaide became his patrons in 1831. His Bombardment of Algiers is now in the National Maritime Museum.

Rudolf Eickemeyer Jr. took up photography to document his father's inventions. He bought his first camera in February 1884 and photographed his sister the next day. His father disapproved of a career in photography, so he kept working in the family firm for years. In 1895 he joined the Carbon Studio in Manhattan and became known for portraits of high-society women, among them Evelyn Nesbit. That year he and Alfred Stieglitz became the first Americans admitted to the Linked Ring. His photographs won dozens of medals around the world.

Carel Dake taught at the Rijksakademie, the State Academy of Fine Arts. His students there included Lizzy Ansingh, Tine Baanders, Guillaume Eberhard, Germ de Jong, Lou Loeber and Johanna Pieneman. He also belonged to the artistic society Arti et Amicitiae and served as its president from 1892 to 1896. He was a Dutch painter and professor, and he died in 1918.

Raymond Lafage died in Lyon at 28, on his way to a second stay in Italy. He studied with Jean-Pierre Rivalz and taught Rivalz's son Antoine and the painter François Boitard. On his first trip to Italy he drew after Italian masters. According to Houbraken, he once drew a crowd in a tavern by turning random scratches on a piece of paper into a complicated Pharaoh entering the Red Sea in two hours. His student Boitard could repeat the trick, but not quite as well. He is notable for mythological prints and drawings.

Anton Karinger painted landscapes and seascapes, mostly views of Carinthia and the Adriatic coast, and he also wrote poems. He studied under Steinfeld in Vienna. His View of Mount Triglav from Bohinj, one of several paintings of the mountain, became a symbol of the Carinthian Slovene people. It is part of the core collection of the National Gallery of Slovenia. He lived from 1829 to 1870.

Carlo Cignani came from a noble family with limited resources in Bologna. He studied first under Battista Cairo and later under Francesco Albani, whose most famous disciple he became. His new manner brought a gentle, reflective, intimate mood to Bolognese painting, in a break with the more energetic earlier classicism. Correggio and Melozzo da Forlì influenced him strongly. His Assumption of the Virgin in the cupola of the church of the Madonna del Fuoco at Forlì occupied him for some twenty years. In 1681 he returned to Bologna from Parma.

Cornelis Vroom followed his father, the painter Hendrick Cornelisz Vroom, into the trade. He joined the Haarlem Guild of St. Luke in 1634. His son Jacob Cornelisz Vroom became a painter too. Like his father, he is best known for landscapes and seascapes. Houbraken listed him in 1718 among the good landscape painters of Haarlem, along with Salomon van Ruysdael. He was a strong influence on fellow Haarlem landscape painter Jacob van Ruisdael.

David Octavius Hill formed the Hill and Adamson studio with the engineer and photographer Robert Adamson, and between 1843 and 1847 they pioneered many aspects of photography in Scotland. Before that he painted landscapes. He learned lithography at the School of Design in Edinburgh and published an album of views, Sketches of Scenery in Perthshire. With other dissatisfied artists, he helped set up a separate Scottish Academy. He illustrated editions of Walter Scott and Robert Burns. From 1836 the Royal Scottish Academy paid him a salary as secretary.

Emanuel Larsen specialized in marine painting under Christoffer Wilhelm Eckersberg at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts. In 1845 the Statens Museum for Kunst bought his Morning off the Coast of Zealand, and that year he also sailed on a naval ship to the Faroe Islands and Iceland. The influential Christian Jürgensen Thomsen praised his paintings for an eye for the fresh, open life at sea, and said his ships appear to move. Larsen was probably the Danish artist least influenced by foreign works, despite his interest in Dutch marine art. He died after a short illness.

Emilio Sala showed his Expulsion of the Jews from Spain at the Exposition Universelle of 1889, only to find that the French public no longer cared for historical works. He took it to Spain, where it was better received. In 1890 he gave up that subject for genre scenes, landscapes and illustrating. He was born in Alcoy to a family of merchants and first studied in Valencia with his cousin Plácido Francés. He won First Prize at the National Exhibition of Fine Arts in 1878. Many of his works appeared in the magazine Blanco y Negro.

Emmanuel Tzanes came from Rethymno on Crete and became a priest. After the Ottomans conquered the town he fled and spent eight years in Corfu, painting many icons, sometimes with Philotheos Skoufos. In 1655 he moved to Venice, where he offered to paint the church of San Giorgio dei Greci for free but was turned down in favor of Skoufos. He succeeded Skoufos as its priest in 1660 and served for twenty years. His icons follow the Cretan school with Venetian influences, and more than 130 of them survive. The most popular is The Holy Towel, finished in 1659.

Ferdinand von Piloty II began as a painter but soon turned to lithography. From 1808 to 1815 he made 423 lithographs with Johann Nepomuk Strixner, published as Les oeuvres lithographiques par Strixner, Piloty et Comp. With Joseph Löhle he later produced a series of copies from the Alte Pinakothek and the Schleissheim Gallery. When Gottlieb Bodmer died in 1837, the two of them continued publishing his works. Piloty was born in Homburg, died in Munich, and was the father of the painter Karl von Piloty.

Antwerp was the home of the Tassaert family. Philip Joseph Tassaert painted and engraved mezzotints, and he died in London. His brother Jean-Pierre-Antoine was a sculptor who worked in Antwerp and London, then in Paris and Berlin. The family produced painters, sculptors, illustrators and art dealers, some of whom settled or worked in France and Prussia in the 17th and 18th centuries.
